claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution in equiatomic, multielement HEA nanoparticles at lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature toward 1923 K makes atomic diffusion barriers surmountable.
Activated atomic diffusion overcomes configurational-entropy stabilization.
Activated atomic diffusion permits elemental rearrangement and segregation in the HEA nanoparticles.
Elemental segregation results in secondary-phase nucleation or phase separation.
The starting nanoparticles contain at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and are initially a single-phase solid solution.
Below a material-dependent temperature threshold, the nanoparticles retain their single-phase solid-solution structure.
Above that threshold, diffraction will reveal secondary phases.
Above that threshold, elemental mapping will reveal compositional inhomogeneity or segregation.
Protective surface treatments can alter diffusion kinetics and therefore change the predicted stability boundary.
A non-reactive atmosphere can alter diffusion kinetics and produce deviations from the prediction.
The segregation threshold may depend on nanoparticle size.
The segregation threshold may depend on alloy composition.
The segregation threshold may depend on nanoparticle surface characteristics.
Temperature will be varied stepwise from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions.
Retention of a homogeneous single phase with no detectable segregation after exceeding the putative threshold would falsify the proposed diffusion-activated breakdown.
